defaults.notes: Ogni run: Context Assembler reale -> Generator -> Validator -> (repair)*. Si registra quanti documenti sono serviti (1-3), i codici di errore incontrati per run (indicano regole del prompt poco chiare) e l'usage con cache_read_tokens. sources_copied_exactly: resource_id, title e url identici a quelli del caso. topic_glossary_copied_exactly: ogni voce del documento con la stessa key di una del Topic ha key, term, definition e avoid identici. numbers_need_citation: ogni paragrafo, callout o feedback che contiene una cifra fuori da `codice` porta almeno una citazione [^key] oppure la cifra compare nella formulazione di un esempio ipotetico segnalato (controllo euristico, da rivedere a mano sui falliti). Fase 9: aggiunti controlli sui difetti trovati nelle due lezioni reali (docs/design/review-mvp.md, problemi 1, 2, 6, 7): rapporto in caratteri delle opzioni, risposta del vuoto nel testo adiacente, chiusura attiva, confronto di codice con missing_component, budget di token. Il Validator reale oggi ammette 3 parole di differenza e non guarda i caratteri: i controlli qui sono più severi di proposito, per misurare se il prompt basta. Run reale 2026-11-09: prosa osservata ~160 parole con la lezione completa, quindi il minimo è 150. Falsi positivi noti del runner (risposte cortissime come `si`, `r`): non inseguirli nel prompt. Fase 12: i piani fissi sono stati portati alla forma nuova (concetti con `example`, `steps`, `pitfall`; `document_sections: []`; `estimated_minutes` dalla formula) mantenendo il contenuto didattico; dove c'era un solo concetto ne è stato aggiunto un secondo coerente con la fonte (rust_second_lesson_recall_and_link: `&mut`; strength_thin_sources: recupero tra le sedute; preference_more_practice: modifiche dopo `git add`; fill_blank_no_leak: copia dei tipi semplici). Le soglie di lunghezza sono quelle della Fase 12 (`prose_words` 1200-2200, `sections` 3-6, `closing_summary_words_max` 60, `glossary_entries_max` 12, `output_tokens` 14000; il caso preference_more_practice 1200-1700), con il conteggio §9; i controlli di contenuto sono invariati. Il caso strength_thin_sources ha ora un prerequisito `general`: la lezione avrà la sezione di richiamo. Dal 2026-11-11 (decisione del proprietario) i piani fissi hanno 4-5 concetti (4 con un prerequisito `general`) con concetti aggiunti coerenti con la fonte del caso; i controlli di contenuto sono invariati, `sections` e `min_exercises` sono stati adattati. `estimated_minutes` lo calcola il backend.

mission.why: I want to stop fighting the compiler and understand its error messages.
success: I read a "borrow of moved value" message and can tell which line moved the value
I choose between passing by value and passing a reference
mission.starting_point: I already know how to program in Python.

plan.title: When a variable stops being valid
plan.objective: Be able to predict whether a Rust variable is still usable after an assignment.
plan.why_now: First step toward the criterion "read the borrow of moved value message": you need to know what moves the value.

prerequisites.statement: Can declare variables and call functions in an imperative language

concepts.name: move
concepts.key_point: Assigning a String moves ownership: the original variable is no longer usable.
concepts.example: let a = String::from("hello"); let b = a; println!("{}", a); does not compile: the value was moved into `b`.
steps: `String::from` creates a value that owns its bytes on the heap, and `a` is its owner.
`let b = a;` transfers ownership to `b`.
From then on `a` is no longer usable and the compiler rejects any later use.
concepts.pitfall: Thinking that `let b = a;` makes a copy of the String and leaves `a` valid.

concepts.name: copying simple types
concepts.key_point: Types like i32 are duplicated and stay valid.
concepts.example: let n = 7; let m = n; println!("{}", n); compiles: `n` is still 7 after the assignment.
steps: `i32` is a simple type that lives entirely on the stack.
`let m = n;` duplicates its value.
Both variables stay valid.
concepts.pitfall: Thinking that copying applies to every type, `String` included.

concepts.name: passing a String to a function
concepts.key_point: Passing a `String` to a function moves it into the parameter: after the call the caller's variable is no longer usable.
concepts.example: `fn consume(s: String) { println!("{}", s); }` called with `let name = String::from("Ada"); consume(name); println!("{}", name);`: the last line does not compile.
steps: `name` owns the string before the call.
`consume(name)` moves ownership into the parameter `s`.
At the end of the function `s` goes out of scope and the string is freed.
Using `name` after the call is using a moved variable: error.
concepts.pitfall: Thinking that a function that receives a `String` only looks at it and the caller finds it intact.

concepts.name: duplicating with clone
concepts.key_point: `clone` makes an explicit copy of the value: afterwards original and copy are both valid, but the copy has a cost.
concepts.example: `let a = String::from("sea"); let b = a.clone(); println!("{} {}", a, b);` compiles and prints `sea sea`.
steps: `a.clone()` allocates a new string with the same bytes.
`b` owns the copy, `a` owns the original: no move.
Both variables stay usable, at the price of one more allocation.
concepts.pitfall: Thinking that `clone` is free and should be put everywhere to silence the compiler.

introduce.hint: rule that every value has a single owner

exercises.purpose: predict the outcome of a String assignment
predict which lines after the call of a function that takes a `String` compile
explain why after `clone` both variables stay valid and after a move they do not

rubric.text: The lesson serves a single capability (predicting validity after an assignment); no borrowing, lifetimes or other topics.
At least one required exercise asks to predict (not just recognise a definition).
The case of at least one exercise differs from the example shown in the explanation's code.
Quiz distractors represent plausible misconceptions and every feedback says why the option looked reasonable.
Every new term is defined in the glossary and used as [[key]] at first mention, before the concept that needs it.
Claims about the rules of Rust carry a citation and no details (version numbers, verbatim quotes) appear that the given sources cannot support.

The open_answer rubric is self-sufficient: it lists key points, typical mistakes with the wrong belief they reveal, and how to treat partial answers; the question does not depend on blocks the grader cannot see.
Sober tone: no praise, no judgement, no "simply/obviously".

No exercise has its answer in the surrounding text: for every fill_blank, the code caption, the section title and the adjacent paragraph say what to observe but do not contain the value of the blank; no quiz has the correct answer given verbatim above.

The final section closes with a checklist of 2-3 concrete actions to take in one's own code (tied to the mission, not repetitions of the exercises) and a summary of at most 2 sentences that does not repeat the exercise answers.
The lesson contains nothing beyond the plan: no superfluous section, callout, glossary term or exercise, and no explanation repeated in two places.
All learner-facing text (headings, paragraphs, captions, quiz options, feedback, checklist) is in English; only code and identifiers are not.

concepts.name: move

concepts.example: let s1 = String::from("rust"); let s2 = s1; println!("{}", s1); does not compile: the value was moved into `s2`.
steps: `s1` owns the value on the heap.
`let s2 = s1;` transfers ownership to `s2`.

concepts.name: copying simple types
concepts.key_point: Types like `i32` are duplicated on assignment and the original variable stays valid.
concepts.example: let n = 7; let m = n; println!("{}", n); compiles: `n` is still 7.
steps: `i32` lives entirely on the stack.

concepts.name: passing a String to a function
concepts.key_point: Passing a `String` to a function moves it into the parameter: after the call the caller's variable is no longer usable.
concepts.example: `fn show(t: String) { println!("{}", t); }` called with `let title = String::from("Dune"); show(title); println!("{}", title);`: the last line does not compile.
steps: `title` owns the string before the call.
`show(title)` moves ownership into the parameter `t`.
After the call `title` is moved: using it is an error.
concepts.pitfall: Thinking that a function that receives a `String` only looks at it and the caller finds it intact.

concepts.name: duplicating with clone
concepts.key_point: `clone` makes an explicit copy: afterwards original and copy are both valid, but the copy has a cost.
concepts.example: `let a = String::from("sail"); let b = a.clone(); println!("{} {}", a, b);` compiles and prints `sail sail`.
steps: `a.clone()` allocates a new string with the same bytes.
`a` and `b` each have their own value: no move.
Both stay usable, at the price of one more allocation.
concepts.pitfall: Thinking that `clone` is free and should be put everywhere to silence the compiler.
